title: Technical deep dive: Quickstart template observability (OTel) + SLOs
next_steps: Redwood to share the template observability hooks reference (span attributes/metrics) and the dashboard pack JSON export.
Arcadia to confirm preferred backend(s) for OTLP (Datadog vs Grafana Tempo/Mimir) and provide endpoint/auth constraints.
Redwood to send recommended starter alerts (burn-rate + latency + tool failures) with suggested thresholds and runbook snippets.
Arcadia to run the local docker-compose collector + sample traffic and validate trace/metric redaction meets internal requirements.
Follow-up 45 min session next week focused on Arcadia’s SLO targets and mapping to Redwood’s dashboards.
transcript_text:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-12
Start time: 2:03 PM PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Renee Sullivan, Allison Grant, Sergio Costa, Christine Wong
Arcadia Search: Maya Rios, Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Samir Patel

Summary (auto-generated)
Arcadia’s platform team reviewed the OpenTelemetry traces and metrics emitted by Redwood’s RAG + agents quickstart templates, with a focus on what is collected by default, how redaction works, and how to operationalize the included dashboard pack and recommended alerts. Redwood walked through span hierarchy, required attributes (including request ID correlation), metric naming/dimensions, and cardinality guardrails. Arcadia asked about Datadog vs Grafana backends, SLO alerting strategy, and security controls around prompt/logging.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Template OTel architecture (traces, metrics, logs) and collector deployment
- Span naming conventions and required attributes
- Metrics: latency, tokens, cache hit, retrieval/tool error rates
- Dashboard pack overview (RAG latency breakdown, tool failure rate, retrieval hit rate, token economics)
- SLO and alerting recommendations (burn rate, p95 latency, error budgets)
- Redaction rules and security considerations

Action items (auto-generated)
- Allison Grant: Send span/metric reference doc + attribute allowlist guidance by 2025-03-14
- Sergio Costa: Export dashboards and alert rules pack + version info by 2025-03-14
- Christine Wong: Provide SLO starter set and notes on avoiding noisy alerts by 2025-03-18
- Maya Rios: Confirm OTLP destination and auth method (Datadog vs Grafana) by 2025-03-19
- Priya Nair: Review redaction approach and confirm compliance constraints (PII/prompt retention) by 2025-03-19

Questions (auto-generated)
- Do the templates ever export prompt/response bodies as span attributes or logs by default?
- What metric labels are safe vs high-cardinality risk?
- How do we correlate a user-facing error to a Redwood request ID and a trace?
- What are the recommended alert thresholds for tool failures and retrieval empty results?

Transcript

[00:00] Renee Sullivan: Cool, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is pretty narrow: walk through what the quickstart templates emit in OpenTelemetry—traces, metrics, logs—how the dashboard pack expects those signals, and then what we recommend for SLOs and alerts. Allison and Sergio are the experts here, and Christine will keep us honest on the SRE side.

[00:22] Maya Rios: Perfect. We’re trying to decide if we can take your template and basically drop it into our platform standards. We already have an OTel collector pattern, but our big worry is, one, cardinality explosions and two, any accidental prompt logging.

[00:37] Allison Grant: Yep. Those are the right worries. High level: templates are instrumented with OpenTelemetry SDKs in-app, exporting OTLP to a collector. The collector config we ship includes redaction processors and an attribute allowlist. By default, we do not record prompt content, tool arguments, or tool outputs as span attributes.

[00:58] Priya Nair: Just to be super clear—“by default” means like, literally out-of-the-box if an engineer clones it?

[01:03] Allison Grant: Correct. Out-of-the-box, the template spans include things like route name, model name, status, timing, and a request ID. The logs are structured and run through a redaction helper that strips common secret patterns and anything that looks like an API key. But prompt text is not included in logs either.

[01:25] Jordan Lee: When you say request ID, is that your gateway request id? Or like the app’s request id?

[01:30] Sergio Costa: Both can exist, but we standardize on a field called redwood.request_id. That’s extracted from the Redwood API response headers. Then we also have trace_id and span_id from OTel. The templates try to propagate redwood.request_id into logs and as a span attribute so you can pivot in your logging tool.

[01:53] Samir Patel: So if I’m debugging “bad answer” I still need some sort of prompt capture, right? But you’re saying it’s opt-in.

[02:00] Allison Grant: Exactly. We’ve seen teams do prompt capture into a separate secure store, not into telemetry. Our default guidance is: don’t put raw prompts into logs, metrics, or traces. If you need quality debugging, use a gated “debug mode” where prompts are stored with retention controls and access control.

[02:22] Renee Sullivan: Maybe we can jump into the concrete span tree, because that’s usually the fastest way to align.

[02:27] Allison Grant: Sure. For the RAG + agents template, a typical request produces:
- An inbound server span: something like “http.server” or framework equivalent.
- A child span: “rag.request” (we use a redwood.quickstart prefix in some places; transcription might vary).
- Under that, you’ll see “rag.retrieve” for retrieval.
- Under retrieve, if you’re using the default vector adapter, you’ll see “vector.query” or “db.query” depending on the library.
- Then the LLM spans: “llm.generate” and for agent loops “agent.step” spans per iteration.
- Tool calls are “tool.call” spans, plus “tool.validate” if schema validation runs.

[03:10] Maya Rios: Do you use the OTel semantic conventions for genAI? There’s a draft spec floating around.

[03:15] Allison Grant: We follow a mix. We keep compatibility with standard OTel attributes where possible, but we also have Redwood-specific attributes because support needs consistency across languages. So you’ll see:
- llm.system = "redwood"
- llm.model = the model identifier
- llm.operation = "chat" or "generate"
- redwood.route = route name (low cardinality)
- redwood.template = template slug, like "rag-agent"
- redwood.template_version = the template release version
And we keep anything user-specific either out of telemetry or hashed.

[03:49] Jordan Lee: What about tenant IDs? We’re multi-tenant.

[03:52] Sergio Costa: Recommended pattern is a stable tenant key but hashed, and only if you really need it. More commonly we recommend tags like environment, service.name, deployment, and route. Tenants can blow up cardinality.

[04:08] Priya Nair: And do you emit user IDs in any form?

[04:11] Allison Grant: Not by default. The template includes a place to add “enduser.id” or “app.user_id_hash” but it’s commented out with warnings.

[04:22] Renee Sullivan: Jordan, you mentioned you already have a collector. Do you want to talk about your backend? Datadog, Grafana, something else?

[04:29] Jordan Lee: We’re mostly Datadog today. But some teams use Grafana Tempo + Mimir for cost reasons. We can support OTLP either way. Our pain point is making sure the metric names line up, and we avoid high-cardinality tags.

[04:46] Sergio Costa: Great. Metric set we require for the dashboards is intentionally small.
Core metrics (names approximate, but consistent prefixes):
- request_latency_ms (histogram)
- llm_latency_ms (histogram)
- retrieval_latency_ms (histogram)
- tool_latency_ms (histogram)
- tokens_in (counter)
- tokens_out (counter)
- request_errors_total (counter)
- tool_errors_total (counter)
- retrieval_empty_total (counter)
- cache_hit_total / cache_miss_total (if caching is enabled)

[05:22] Maya Rios: Dimensions on those?

[05:24] Sergio Costa: Kept low-cardinality:
- service.name
- env (prod/staging)
- redwood.route
- llm.model (bounded set)
- status_code bucket or error_class
We strongly recommend not tagging with document IDs, query text, tool arguments, or arbitrary URLs.

[05:49] Christine Wong: And to underline it: alerting gets unusable if your labels are like “customer_id=12345” across everything. We’d rather have clean service-level alerts and then drill down by trace.

[06:03] Jordan Lee: On error_class, what’s the taxonomy? We’ve been bitten by “everything is just 500.”

[06:10] Allison Grant: The template uses a small error taxonomy for logs and spans. Example classes:
- auth_error
- quota_error (429)
- network_error
- timeout
- upstream_5xx
- tool_schema_error
- tool_runtime_error
- retrieval_error
- retrieval_empty
We attach error_class as a span attribute and log field when possible.

[06:40] Samir Patel: “Retrieval empty” is not always an error for us, sometimes it means “no results, answer from model.”

[06:46] Allison Grant: That’s fair. We treat it as a signal not necessarily a failure. The dashboard has a panel “retrieval hit rate.” You can decide whether you alert on it. Some teams alert only when it changes sharply, not when it’s low.

[07:05] Renee Sullivan: Maybe we can look at the dashboards pack. Sergio, can you summarize what’s included?

[07:11] Sergio Costa: Sure. The template dashboard pack has three primary dashboards:
1) RAG Request Overview: request volume, error rate, p50/p95 latency, breakdown of retrieve vs generate.
2) Agent + Tools Health: tool call rate, tool error rate by error_class, tool latency, agent iterations distribution.
3) Token Economics: tokens in/out, cost proxy panels, cache hit rate if enabled, and a “top routes by token burn” panel.

[07:40] Maya Rios: “Cost proxy” meaning you multiply tokens by a price?

[07:44] Sergio Costa: Exactly. We don’t assume your exact pricing; there’s a variable in the dashboard or you can compute a derived metric in your backend.

[07:52] Jordan Lee: How do you handle sampling for traces? Datadog costs can spike.

[07:58] Allison Grant: Default is head-based sampling at a modest rate for production, and always-on for local dev. Also, we bias to keep traces when error occurs. The collector config includes tail-sampling examples, but we don’t enable tail sampling by default because it’s more moving parts.

[08:18] Christine Wong: Recommended practical approach: start with 5–10% trace sampling in prod, keep 100% of error traces, and if you’re doing SLO investigations, temporarily bump sampling for a route.

[08:32] Priya Nair: Can you guarantee redaction at the collector? Like if an engineer accidentally adds a prompt attribute.

[08:38] Allison Grant: We can’t guarantee someone won’t code around it, but we provide guardrails. The collector pipeline we ship uses an attributes processor to drop any attribute keys that match patterns like “prompt”, “input”, “completion”, “messages”, plus a strict allowlist mode. In allowlist mode, only known safe keys pass through.

[09:06] Maya Rios: We like allowlist. That’s our standard.

[09:09] Allison Grant: Same here. It’s the safest for templates.

[09:14] Jordan Lee: How do logs fit in? Are you emitting logs via OTel logs or just stdout JSON?

[09:21] Sergio Costa: Template apps log JSON to stdout by default with correlation fields: trace_id, span_id, redwood.request_id, error_class. You can route that to your logging stack. We also provide an option to emit OTel logs, but most customers prefer stdout + collector.

[09:45] Samir Patel: I want to understand the “LLM span.” Are you wrapping the SDK call? Or is it inside your gateway?

[09:52] Allison Grant: In the template, we wrap the Redwood SDK call in a span. It’s client-side instrumentation. We capture timing and status, plus model and route. We also propagate trace context via headers so if you have downstream visibility, you can connect it.

[10:14] Jordan Lee: Does Redwood propagate trace context through your API? Like will you echo it back?

[10:19] Allison Grant: We support request ID correlation strongly. End-to-end distributed tracing into Redwood’s internal spans is limited. But you get stable request IDs, and you get client-side spans that cover what you control. For most teams, that’s enough to triage latency and error issues.

[10:39] Maya Rios: Okay. Let’s talk SLOs. Christine, what do you recommend as “starter”? Our stakeholders are asking for an uptime number.

[10:48] Christine Wong: Starter set:
- Availability SLO: successful responses / total, where success excludes auth failures and maybe excludes client cancellations.
- Latency SLO: p95 end-to-end request latency under X ms for your main route(s).
- Tooling SLO: tool error rate under a threshold (like <1–2%) if tools are critical.
Then use burn-rate alerting instead of naive threshold alerts.

[11:19] Jordan Lee: What’s “burn rate” in this context?

[11:22] Christine Wong: It’s alerting on how fast you’re consuming error budget. Example: 99.9% availability SLO means 0.1% errors. If you start seeing 1% errors, you’re burning 10x. We use short-window and long-window burn rate alerts to avoid noise.

[11:46] Sergio Costa: The alert rules pack we ship includes both. Something like: 14-day SLO with 1-hour and 6-hour burn-rate alert windows.

[11:56] Maya Rios: Do you have recommended thresholds for tool errors? Our tools might be flaky.

[12:02] Allison Grant: We suggest starting with:
- tool_errors / tool_calls > 2% for 10 minutes = warning
- > 5% for 5 minutes = critical
But only if the tool is part of your main path. If it’s “nice to have,” make it informational.

[12:22] Samir Patel: And for retrieval empty rate, you said don’t alert. But what do people do?

[12:28] Sergio Costa: We’ve seen a “change detection” alert: if retrieval hit rate drops by, say, 30% relative to last 24h baseline, alert. That catches broken indexing pipelines.

[12:43] Jordan Lee: What about token spikes? That’s cost.

[12:46] Christine Wong: Token spikes are great as anomaly alerts, but do it carefully. We recommend per-route token_out p95 or average, plus a “max_tokens cap hit rate” metric. If cap hit rate suddenly increases, prompts changed or model behavior changed.

[13:08] Priya Nair: On the security side, do your dashboards or logs include any payload? I’m asking because some vendors auto-capture HTTP bodies.

[13:17] Allison Grant: Good point. We do not enable HTTP body capture. We explicitly disable it in the sample instrumentation. We capture method and route pattern, not full URL with query params.

[13:34] Maya Rios: Can you talk about cardinality again? Specifically, model name. We might A/B models.

[13:40] Sergio Costa: Model name is fine if it’s a small, bounded set. We’ve seen teams add “model_version_hash” as a label and then it explodes. Our recommendation: model is okay; model_version only if it’s like “v1/v2” and not a unique build id.

[14:03] Jordan Lee: How do you tag “template traffic” versus normal app traffic? We want to evaluate adoption.

[14:10] Renee Sullivan: There’s an optional convention: templates can add a header or tag that indicates “origin=quickstart” plus template name/version. But we learned some corporate proxies reject unknown headers, so it’s opt-in and can also be done as a client-side attribute rather than a network header.

[14:31] Priya Nair: Yeah, we’ve had proxies block stuff. We’d prefer no new headers.

[14:35] Allison Grant: Then do it purely as telemetry attributes in your app. Like redwood.template and redwood.template_version on spans/metrics.

[14:49] Samir Patel: On metrics, can you even set attributes for a counter without cardinality problems? Like version.

[14:55] Sergio Costa: Version is okay if you have like, a handful. If every dev is running a different patch, you’ll pay for it. For production, we recommend you pin to a release and then version labels remain bounded.

[15:12] Maya Rios: How do upgrades work? Is there a story to keep template_version from going crazy?

[15:18] Renee Sullivan: The templates are versioned releases. When you scaffold, we stamp a version in the repo. In prod you should be deploying a pinned release, not “latest from main.”

[15:32] Jordan Lee: Okay. Let’s walk through a typical incident. Suppose p95 latency spikes. What do we see in your dashboard?

[15:40] Sergio Costa: In the “RAG Request Overview,” we show stacked latency: retrieval vs LLM. If LLM latency spikes, you’ll also see llm_latency_ms increase and potentially upstream_5xx. If retrieval spikes, you’ll see retrieval_latency_ms, plus maybe retrieval_error. If tool is slow, tool_latency_ms plus “agent.step” duration goes up.

[16:08] Allison Grant: And the trace is the source of truth. A single trace shows you: did we spend 800ms in vector query, or 2 seconds in the model generation, or are we looping tools.

[16:22] Christine Wong: One SRE note: ensure timeouts are set so you don’t have zombie requests. The templates set reasonable timeouts and retries. That affects your latency distribution and your error budget.

[16:35] Jordan Lee: How do retries show up? I hate when retries hide in the dark.

[16:40] Allison Grant: Good call. Each retry attempt is a span event or a child span depending on language. We mark attempt count as a span attribute (low cardinality) and we log “retrying” with reason=timeout/network. So you can see that “LLM call took 3.2s” but it was actually two attempts.

[17:05] Samir Patel: For streaming responses, do you record time-to-first-token? That’s what users feel.

[17:10] Sergio Costa: Yes, we include a metric “ttft_ms” (time to first token) when streaming is enabled, and a span event on the llm.generate span. Some SDKs call it first_byte.

[17:28] Maya Rios: That’s huge for us.

[17:31] Priya Nair: Streaming also complicates logging because you can’t log the entire response body anyway. So that’s good.

[17:40] Renee Sullivan: Can we take a quick detour on where this runs? You asked earlier about collector deployment.

[17:45] Jordan Lee: Yeah—our standard is per-cluster collector, OTLP over gRPC with mTLS.

[17:51] Allison Grant: That works. Templates support OTLP over HTTP or gRPC. Local dev uses docker-compose with a collector that exports to console or to Tempo. For prod, you point to your collector endpoint and provide headers for auth. Again: no payload, just telemetry.

[18:18] Priya Nair: Are there any secrets in env vars that could leak into metrics? Like if someone sets OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS with a token.

[18:26] Allison Grant: We never log those env vars. But you’re right, some systems dump env vars on crash. We add guidance in README: don’t print env, and use secret managers.

[18:40] Christine Wong: Also configure crash reporting carefully. We’ve seen “diagnostics upload includes env.” Don’t do that.

[18:49] Maya Rios: Okay. Another question: do you have a “minimum viable” set of signals required for support? Like if we open a ticket with Redwood.

[18:58] Allison Grant: Minimum we ask for: redwood.request_id, approximate timestamp, model name, and error message. If you have traces, even better, but request ID alone lets our team look up gateway logs on our side.

[19:15] Jordan Lee: Nice. So request ID is critical.

[19:18] Sergio Costa: Exactly. The template tries hard to capture and propagate it.

[19:24] Samir Patel: If our agent tool call fails schema validation, what does the user see? And what do we see in telemetry?

[19:31] Allison Grant: User sees a friendly error that tool output didn’t match schema, plus a remediation hint. Telemetry: tool.validate span with status=error, error_class=tool_schema_error, and a truncated message. We don’t include full tool output in telemetry.

[19:55] Priya Nair: “Truncated message” doesn’t contain tool output, right?

[19:58] Allison Grant: Correct. It’s like “schema validation failed: missing field ‘id’.” Not the payload.

[20:06] Jordan Lee: How about exemplars linking metrics to traces? We use that with histograms.

[20:12] Sergio Costa: If your backend supports exemplars, yes. We set trace_id on histogram observations where possible. Datadog has partial support; Grafana stack is better there.

[20:28] Maya Rios: On alerts. We have an internal rule: no more than 5 paging alerts per service. What would you pick?

[20:35] Christine Wong: For a single RAG service, my default paging set is:
1) Availability burn-rate (fast)
2) Availability burn-rate (slow)
3) Latency SLO burn-rate (fast)
4) Upstream 5xx elevated (only if it’s actionable)
5) Tool failures critical (if tools are critical path)
Everything else is ticket or dashboard.

[21:08] Jordan Lee: I like that. And runbooks?

[21:11] Christine Wong: We include simple runbook bullets: check whether it’s retrieval vs model, check retry counts, check tool error_class, check rate limiting (429) vs 5xx.

[21:25] Maya Rios: Speaking of 429, do templates handle rate limits gracefully? We’ve seen thundering herds.

[21:32] Allison Grant: They do exponential backoff with jitter and a cap. Also concurrency defaults are conservative now. We also log error_class=quota_error and status_code=429 so you can see it.

[21:50] Jordan Lee: Do you recommend alerting on 429?

[21:53] Christine Wong: Not as paging unless it’s unexpected. It might be self-inflicted. Better as a warning / dashboard. If 429 drives your availability SLO, it will show up there.

[22:08] Samir Patel: If retrieval is in a separate service, do you still cover it?

[22:13] Allison Grant: Yes, you’d instrument retrieval service with OTel too. The template’s “rag.retrieve” span would become a client span to that service. Then you get distributed tracing across your boundary.

[22:30] Maya Rios: Okay, this is tracking. One more: does the dashboard pack assume Prometheus naming? Or OTel naming?

[22:37] Sergio Costa: We ship it in a neutral way as much as possible, but there are variants. For Grafana, we provide PromQL examples; for Datadog, we provide query equivalents. The canonical source is OTel metric names.

[22:55] Jordan Lee: Great. We’ll probably start with Datadog.

[23:00] Priya Nair: I want the collector config that does allowlisting. Can you send that?

[23:04] Allison Grant: Yes. We’ll send the “production” collector example with attributes allowlist and redaction processors.

[23:12] Renee Sullivan: Let’s pause for any other questions before we wrap.

[23:17] Maya Rios: I think we’re good. Next step is we’ll run the template locally, point to our dev collector, and see what shows up. If it matches what you described, we’ll proceed.

[23:28] Jordan Lee: And we’ll need the dashboards and alert rules, otherwise we’ll reinvent it.

[23:33] Sergio Costa: Got it. I’ll send exports and a quick “how to import” note.

[23:38] Christine Wong: And I’ll send a starter SLO spec—what to measure, and example burn-rate alerts.

[23:44] Priya Nair: Plus a note confirming no prompt capture by default. That’s what I’ll need for internal review.

[23:50] Allison Grant: Yep, I’ll include that explicitly.

[23:55] Renee Sullivan: Perfect. Thanks all. We’ll follow up with links and schedule the next session.

[END]

Note: Transcript timestamps after ~24 minutes may be truncated due to export settings; key technical content captured in the first half of the recording.
